text: 49 The brain doesn’t merely process external inputs; it continuously monitors and integrates the internal state of the body. In this framing, consciousness may not be fully realized in disembodied code. It is the dialogue between mind and body—the loop of prediction, sensation, adjustment—that gives rise to what we experience as awareness. In his work, Antonio Damasio proposes that consciousness arises in three nested stages: 50 1. Protoself —the base representation of the internal physical state 2. Core consciousness —the awareness of one’s body in the present moment 3. Extended consciousness —the autobiographical self, woven through time (with memory) These stages aren’t metaphysical; they are physiological. They arise from the interplay between body, brain, and world. By applying Damasio’s biological framework to artificial systems, we can see a potential road map for the emergence of a digital self. If AI is ever to develop something akin to self-awareness, overlaying Damasio’s biological consciousness framework suggests that it must move beyond pure computation and toward systems that sense, prioritize, and remember. If Damasio’s framework were applied to AI, then AI systems confined to virtual environments may always lack a crucial component of consciousness: the lived experience of a body in motion, under constraint, navigating survival. But if you turn that around, when AI enters the physical world, it just may begin to develop a protoself, a core self, and an autobiographical self, as defined by Damasio. And that seems highly akin to consciousness. Whether this would constitute consciousness in any meaningful sense remains an open question—one that pushes the boundaries of both neuroscience and philosophy. This extrapolation of human consciousness theory to artificial systems is a leap that consciousness researchers would acknowledge is highly speculative. We may be entirely wrong about the requirements for, or even the possibility of, any form of machine consciousness, however limited. Consciousness is a tricky subject. We will dive into that more deeply soon. But for now, let’s continue the exploration of AI embodiment through robotics. The Robotic Amygdala The transition from theory to practice is already underway. In 2024, researchers at the Polytechnic University of Turin in Italy demonstrated exactly this kind of development. Alessandro Rizzo and doctoral candidate Andrea Usai, consulting with top neuroscientists, designed a control system for robots that emulates a human fear response. 51 The researchers focused on fear because it’s “one of the most studied emotions in neuroscience and, in our view, the one with the greatest potential for robotics. Fear is closely related to self-preservation and rapid responses to danger, both of which are critical for adaptive behavior.” 52 They effectively built a reflex system for robots so they can duck (or avoid collisions) instantly, just as a human would, rather than waiting for a computer vision system to analyze the object first. Their approach mirrors something remarkable about our own biology. In humans, the amygdala doesn’t just process fear—it has direct pathways to motor control that bypass conscious thought initially for speed of response. When a ball flies toward your head, you duck before you’re even aware of seeing it. Your amygdala triggers the physical response milliseconds ahead of your conscious brain catching up to say, “That was a ball.” This is Kahneman’s System 1 in action—part of that massive ratio of unconscious to conscious processing we discussed earlier. Your body is already moving while your conscious mind is still several processing steps behind, analyzing what just happened. This immediate body–brain connection is what kept our ancestors alive when split-second reactions meant the difference between survival and death. And it’s precisely this kind of rapid, preconscious response that the Italian researchers built into their robots. The researchers essentially created this same principle digitally: a controller based on reinforced learning that helps the robot dynamically adjust its priorities and constraints in real time based on the raw data of its surroundings. When tested in simulated environments with moving hazards, the robot with the fear-based programming navigated around dangerous objects with “a wider berth of about 3.1 meters,” whereas conventional robots came within “a harrowing 0.3 and 0.8 meters of dangerous objects.” 53 But remember the story of my son’s executive override. There is a critical question to explore: how the robotic amygdala will connect up to the main AI brain, its executive override function, and how it will develop a healthy mechanism when the fear trigger is not about an instant response, but about a longer-term threat. What are the strategies for the AI brain receiving fear-like inputs from the robotic amygdala to make decisions when dealing with a complex world? We will explore this further in a later section about how AI will prioritize human well-being. It is worth noting that the researchers building this see it as just the beginning. As Rizzo stated, “Looking ahead, it would also be interesting trying to extend the architecture to incorporate multiple emotions … enabling a richer and more nuanced form of adaptive behavior in robotic systems.” 54 Here we see the emergence of artificial emotion not as science fiction, but as engineering. And like their biological counterpart, these systems may need to evolve not just the capacity for rapid response but the wisdom to know when not to respond—the very executive functions that make emotion productive rather than paralyzing. Robotics is merging with machine learning, and the result will be robotic-embodied artificial intelligence. Boston Dynamics builds robots that run, dance, and recover from impact. Tesla’s Optimus project aims to integrate full generative AI into a humanoid form. Each new integration brings with it not just motion but limitation. Weight. Friction. Vulnerability. These constraints could shape behavior in ways that a disembodied AI—functioning purely as software—could not. At present, robotic architectures are often functionally split: Generative large language models perform abstract reasoning and communication, while separate systems manage perception, navigation, and motor execution. This separation reflects both engineering optimization and computational specialization.
